before: SAMPSON. Gregory, I swear, we won't put up with any insults.
after: SAMPSON. Gregory, I swear we won't carry coals for anyone.

before: GREGORY. No, because then we'd be no better than coal carriers.
after: GREGORY. No. That would make us coalmen.

before: SAMPSON. I mean, if we get angry, we'll draw our swords.
after: SAMPSON. I mean, if someone insults us and gets us fired up, we'll draw.

before: SAMPSON. A dog from that house will provoke me to stand my ground. I'll take the upper hand over any man or woman from the Montagues.
after: SAMPSON. Any dog from that house will make me stand my ground. Man or maid, I'll take the wall and make them walk in the gutter.

before: GREGORY. That just shows you're a weak servant, because the weakest always get pushed aside.
after: GREGORY. Then you're a weakling. It's the weakest who gets shoved against the wall.

before: GREGORY. It's a good thing you're not a fish; if you were, you'd be a dried-out nobody. Draw your sword. Here come some of the Montagues.
after: GREGORY. Good thing you're not a fish. You'd be a piece of dried cod. Draw your tool: here come some Montagues.

before: [Exeunt Prince and Attendants; Capulet, Lady Capulet, Tybalt,]
after: [The Prince and his attendants, Capulet, Lady Capulet and Tybalt exit.]

before: PRINCE. Citizens and Servants._]
after: [Citizens and servants exit.]

before: BENVOLIO. I guessed that much when I figured you were in love.
after: BENVOLIO. When I guessed you were in love, my aim was pretty close.

before: ROMEO. Good guess, and she's beautiful.
after: ROMEO. You're a good shot. And the girl I love is fair.

before: BENVOLIO. Then she's sworn to live without love forever?
after: BENVOLIO. So she's sworn to stay chaste?

before: BENVOLIO. I'll prove that theory wrong, or die trying.
after: BENVOLIO. I'll teach you that lesson, or die still owing it to you.

before: CAPULET. And those married so young are often ruined too soon. The earth has swallowed all my children except her. She is my one remaining hope. But go ahead and court her, gentle Paris. Win her heart. My consent depends on hers. If she agrees, then she has my blessing. Tonight I'm holding a party, an old tradition, and I've invited many guests, including people I care about. You're one more welcome addition. Come to my house tonight and you'll see stars walking on earth that make the heavens seem dark. You'll feel the same delight that young men feel when April, beautifully dressed, steps on the heels of limping winter. Among the lovely young women at my party, you'll find your share of joy tonight. Look at them all, see them all, and favor the one who deserves it most. Among the many, my daughter may be counted in number, though perhaps not stand out. Come with me. You there, go around Verona and find the people whose names are written here [gives a paper], and tell them my house and hospitality await their pleasure.
after: CAPULET. And those married so young are often ruined too soon. The earth has swallowed all my children except her. She is my one remaining hope. But go ahead and court her, gentle Paris. Win her heart. My consent depends on hers. If she agrees, then she has my blessing. Tonight I'm holding a party, an old tradition, and I've invited many guests, including people I care about. You're one more welcome addition. Come to my house tonight and you'll see stars walking on earth that light up the dark heavens. You'll feel the same delight that young men feel when April, beautifully dressed, steps on the heels of limping winter. Among the lovely young women at my party, you'll find your share of joy tonight. Look at them all, see them all, and favor the one who deserves it most. Among the many, my daughter may be counted in number, though perhaps not stand out. Come with me. You there, go around Verona and find the people whose names are written here [gives a paper], and tell them my house and hospitality await their pleasure.

before: SERVANT. Find the people whose names are written here! They say the shoemaker should stick to his measuring rod and the tailor to his needle, the fisherman to his paintbrush and the painter to his nets. But I've been sent to find the people whose names are written here, and I can't even read what's written. I'd better find someone who can. Oh, perfect timing!
after: SERVANT. Find the people whose names are written here! There's a saying that the shoemaker should stick to his measuring stick, the tailor to his shoe last, the fisherman to his brush, the painter to his nets. And here I am, sent to find the people on this list when I can't even make out their names. I need someone who can read. Just in time!

before: ROMEO. A bandage leaf is great for that.
after: ROMEO. A plantain leaf is just the thing for that.

before: BENVOLIO. Come on, you only think she's so beautiful because you've never compared her to anyone else. She's only been weighed against herself. But put her on a scale against some other woman I'll show you shining at this party, and she'll barely measure up compared to the one who now seems best.
after: BENVOLIO. Come on, you only think she's so beautiful because you've never compared her to anyone else. She's only been weighed against herself. But put her on a scale against some other woman I'll show you shining at this party, and the girl you think the fairest now will scarcely look fair.

before: [Enter Romeo, Mercutio, Benvolio, with five or six Maskers;]
after: [Romeo, Mercutio and Benvolio enter with five or six masked guests.]

before: Torch-bearers and others.
after: [Torchbearers and others accompany them.]

before: MERCUTIO. If love is rough with you, be rough with love. Fight back against love's sting, and you'll beat it down. Give me a mask to cover my face. A mask over a face that's already a mask. What do I care if some nosy person spots my flaws? These thick eyebrows will do my blushing for me.
after: MERCUTIO. If love plays rough with you, play rough with love. If it pricks you, give it a prick back and beat it down. Give me a mask for my face. [He puts it on.] One mask over another! Who cares if someone spots my flaws? Let these bushy eyebrows blush for me.

before: MERCUTIO. Oh, then I see Queen Mab has visited you. She's the fairy midwife, and she arrives in a shape no bigger than a gemstone on a mayor's finger, drawn by a team of tiny atoms across men's noses as they sleep. Her wagon's spokes are made from long spider legs, the canopy from grasshopper wings. Her harnesses are the finest spider silk, her collars made from moonbeams. Her whip is a cricket's bone, the lash a thin strand. Her driver is a tiny gray-coated gnat, not half as big as a small worm picked from a lazy girl's finger. Her carriage is an empty hazelnut shell, made by the carpenter squirrel or the old grub, fairy coachmakers since time began. And in this tiny state she gallops night after night through lovers' brains, making them dream of love. Over courtiers' knees, making them dream of bowing. Over lawyers' fingers, making them dream of fees. Over ladies' lips, making them dream of kisses — though angry Mab often plagues those lips with blisters because their breath smells of candy. Sometimes she rides over a courtier's nose, and he dreams of sniffing out a political favor. Sometimes she tickles a priest's nose with a pig's tail, and he dreams of getting a bigger parish. Sometimes she drives across a soldier's neck, and he dreams of cutting foreign throats, of battles and ambushes and Spanish swords, of drinking contests five fathoms deep. Then suddenly drums pound in his ear, and he wakes with a start, swears a prayer or two, and falls back asleep. This is the same Mab who tangles horses' manes in the night and bakes the matted knots in dirty hair, which bring bad luck when untangled. This is the spirit that, when girls lie on their backs, presses down on them and teaches them how to bear weight, making them women who carry well. This is she —
after: MERCUTIO. Oh, then I see Queen Mab has visited you. She's the fairy midwife, and she arrives in a shape no bigger than a agate on a city councillor's finger, drawn by a team of tiny atoms across men's noses as they sleep. Her wagon's spokes are made from long spider legs, the canopy from grasshopper wings. Her harnesses are the finest spider silk, her collars made from moonbeams. Her whip is a cricket's bone, the lash a thin strand. Her driver is a tiny gray-coated gnat, not half as big as a small worm picked from a lazy girl's finger. Her carriage is an empty hazelnut shell, made by the carpenter squirrel or the old grub, fairy coachmakers since time began. And in this splendor she gallops night after night through lovers' brains, making them dream of love. Over courtiers' knees, making them dream of bowing. Over lawyers' fingers, making them dream of fees. Over ladies' lips, making them dream of kisses — though angry Mab often plagues those lips with blisters because their breath smells of candy. Sometimes she rides over a courtier's nose, and he dreams of sniffing out a political favor. Sometimes she tickles a priest's nose with a pig's tail, and he dreams of getting a bigger parish. Sometimes she drives across a soldier's neck, and he dreams of cutting foreign throats, of battles and ambushes and Spanish swords, of drinking contests five fathoms deep. Then suddenly drums pound in his ear, and he wakes with a start, swears a prayer or two, and falls back asleep. This is the same Mab who tangles horses' manes in the night and bakes the matted knots in dirty hair, which bring bad luck when untangled. This is the spirit that, when girls lie on their backs, presses down on them and teaches them how to bear weight, making them women who carry well. This is she —

before: Musicians waiting. Enter Servants.
after: [Musicians are waiting. Servants enter.]

before: [To Juliet.] If I profane with my unworthiest hand]
after: [Romeo speaks to Juliet.]

before: ROMEO. This holy shrine, the gentle sin is this: my lips, like two blushing pilgrims, are ready to smooth that rough touch with a tender kiss.
after: ROMEO. If my unworthy hand offends this holy shrine, here's a gentle way to make amends. My lips, two blushing pilgrims, stand ready to smooth that rough touch with a tender kiss.

before: CHORUS. Now his old desire for Rosaline lies on its deathbed, and a young new love is eager to take its place. The beauty he used to sigh and long for, now matched against tender Juliet, isn't beautiful anymore. Now Romeo is loved and loves in return, both equally bewitched by each other's looks. But he must plead his love to someone who is supposed to be his enemy, and she must steal love's sweet rewards from dangerous hooks. Being considered an enemy, he can't approach her to make the kind of vows that lovers swear. And she, equally in love, has even fewer chances to meet her new beloved anywhere. But passion gives them the power and the opportunity to meet, softening extreme hardship with extreme sweetness.
after: CHORUS. [Enters.] Now his old desire for Rosaline lies on its deathbed, and a young new love is eager to take its place. The beauty he used to sigh and long for, now matched against tender Juliet, isn't beautiful anymore. Now Romeo is loved and loves in return, both equally bewitched by each other's looks. But he must plead his love to someone who is supposed to be his enemy, and she must steal love's sweet rewards from dangerous hooks. Being considered an enemy, he can't approach her to make the kind of vows that lovers swear. And she, equally in love, has even fewer chances to meet her new beloved anywhere. But passion gives them strength and time gives them a chance to meet, softening extreme hardship with extreme sweetness.

before: MERCUTIO. If love is blind, it can't hit the target. Now he'll sit under a fruit tree and wish his girlfriend were that kind of fruit that girls laugh about in private. Oh Romeo, if only she were, and you a nice ripe pear! Romeo, good night. I'll go to my little bed. This open field is too cold for me to sleep in. Shall we go?
after: MERCUTIO. If love is blind, it can't hit the mark. Now he'll sit under a medlar tree wishing his sweetheart were the fruit girls call an open arse when they laugh together. Oh Romeo, if only she were that open arse and you a fine long pear! Good night, Romeo. I'm going back to my bed. This field is too cold to sleep in. Shall we go?

before: [Within.] Madam.]
after: NURSE. [From inside.] Miss!

before: [Within.] Madam.]
after: NURSE. [From inside.] Miss!

before: ROMEO. Good morning to you both. What slip did I give you?
after: ROMEO. Good morning to you both. What counterfeit coin did I pass you?

before: MERCUTIO. The dodge, sir, the dodge. Don't you get it?
after: MERCUTIO. The slip, sir, the slip. A false coin, and that's what you gave us when you slipped off!

before: MERCUTIO. It's no less, I tell you. The hand on the clock is right at the stroke of noon.
after: MERCUTIO. It is, I assure you. The naughty hand on the dial is standing straight up at the prick of noon.

before: NURSE. If you are he, sir, I'd like a private word with you.
after: NURSE. If you're the one, sir, I'd like a little confidence with you.

before: BENVOLIO. She'll be inviting him to dinner.
after: BENVOLIO. She means to indict him to dinner!

before: MERCUTIO. A matchmaker! A matchmaker! Hey!
after: MERCUTIO. A bawd! A bawd! A bawd! Tally-ho!

before: MERCUTIO. Not a rabbit, sir — unless it's a stale old rabbit in a Lenten pie, something gray and worn out before it's even finished.
after: MERCUTIO. No hare, sir, unless it's one baked in a Lenten pie and going gray and stale before it's eaten.

before: MERCUTIO. An old gray rabbit, an old gray rabbit, is decent enough during Lent. But a rabbit that's gray is too old to pay for when it grays before it's spent. Romeo, are you coming to your father's house? We'll have dinner there.
after:
MERCUTIO. An old gray hare, an old gray hare,
Makes decent meat in Lent.
But a hoary old hare
Isn't worth the fare
If it goes gray before it's spent.
Romeo, are you coming to your father's? We're dining there.

before: BENVOLIO. If I were as quick to quarrel as you, any man could buy my life insurance for an hour and fifteen minutes.
after: BENVOLIO. If I picked fights the way you do, anyone could buy my whole life outright, in fee simple, for the price of an hour and a quarter.

before: MERCUTIO. An hour and fifteen minutes? Simple!
after: MERCUTIO. Fee simple! You're simple all right!

before: TYBALT. Mercutio, you hang around with Romeo.
after: TYBALT. Mercutio, you're in Romeo's company.

before: MERCUTIO. "Hang around"? What, do you think we're musicians? If you make us out to be musicians, expect to hear nothing but discords. Here's my fiddle bow — here's what will make you dance. God's blood — "hang around"!
after: MERCUTIO. Company? A company of musicians, are we? Then expect nothing but discords. Here is my fiddle bow. This will make you dance! God’s blood, “company”!

before: [Draws.] Alla stoccata carries it away.]
after: MERCUTIO. [Draws his sword.] So a fencing thrust wins the day!

before: [Drawing.] I am for you.]
after: TYBALT. [Draws his sword.] I'll take you on.

before: LADY CAPULET. Tybalt, my cousin! Oh, my brother's child! Oh Prince! Oh husband! The blood of my dear relative has been spilled! Prince, as you are just, demand that Montague blood be shed for ours. Oh cousin, cousin!
after: LADY CAPULET. Tybalt, my own flesh and blood! My brother's son! Oh, Prince! Oh, husband! My dear kinsman's blood is spilled. Prince, if you are just, let Montague blood be shed for ours! Oh, my poor nephew!

before: JULIET. Race faster, you fiery horses of the sun, toward the western horizon. A driver like Phaeton would whip you into the west and bring dark night immediately. Spread your curtain, loving night, so that no prying eyes can see, and Romeo can leap into my arms unnoticed and unseen. Lovers can see well enough to perform their acts of love by their own beauty. Or if love is blind, all the better — it suits the darkness. Come, sober night, dressed all in black, and teach me how to win by losing, playing for a pair of untouched maidenheads. Cover the wild blood rushing to my cheeks with your dark cloak, until shy love grows bold and sees that true love acted upon is simply innocent devotion. Come, night! Come, Romeo! You day within the night! You will lie upon the wings of night, whiter than fresh snow on a raven's back. Come, gentle night. Come, loving, dark-browed night. Give me my Romeo. And when I die, take him and cut him into little stars, and he will make the face of heaven so beautiful that the whole world will fall in love with the night and stop worshiping the garish sun. Oh, I have bought the mansion of love but haven't moved in yet. I've been sold but not yet enjoyed. The wait is as unbearable as the night before a holiday to an impatient child who has new clothes and isn't allowed to wear them yet. Oh, here comes my Nurse. She brings news! And every voice that speaks anything other than Romeo's name is as nothing compared to his heavenly eloquence.
after: JULIET. Race faster, you fiery horses of the sun, toward the western horizon. A driver like Phaeton would whip you into the west and bring dark night immediately. Spread your curtain, loving night, so that no prying eyes can see, and Romeo can leap into my arms unnoticed and unseen. Lovers can see well enough to perform their acts of love by their own beauty. Or if love is blind, all the better — it suits the darkness. Come, sober night, dressed all in black, and teach me how to win by losing, playing for a pair of untouched maidenheads. Cover the wild blood rushing to my cheeks with your dark cloak, until shy love grows bold and sees that true love acted upon is simply innocent devotion. Come, night! Come, Romeo! You day within the night! You will lie upon the wings of night, whiter than fresh snow on a raven's back. Come, gentle night. Come, loving, dark-browed night. Give me my Romeo. And when I die, take him and cut him into little stars, and he will make the face of heaven so beautiful that the whole world will fall in love with the night and stop worshiping the garish sun. Oh, I have bought the mansion of love but haven't moved in yet. I've been sold but not yet enjoyed. The wait is as unbearable as the night before a holiday to an impatient child who has new clothes and isn't allowed to wear them yet. Oh, here comes my Nurse. She brings news! Any tongue that so much as says Romeo's name speaks like an angel.

before: [Knocking within.]
after: [Someone knocks offstage.]

before: [Within.] Let me come in, and you shall know my errand.]
after: NURSE. [From outside.] Let me in and you'll hear what brings me.

before: [Enter Romeo and Juliet.]
after: [Romeo and Juliet enter on the open gallery outside Juliet's room, overlooking the garden.]

before: [Within.] Ho, daughter, are you up?]
after: LADY CAPULET. [From inside.] Daughter, are you up?

before: PARIS. She weeps constantly for Tybalt's death, and so I've barely talked to her about love. Venus doesn't smile in a house of mourning. Now her father thinks it's dangerous for her to give in so completely to grief. In his wisdom, he's rushing our marriage to stop the flood of her tears, which, left alone with too much brooding, may only get worse. Now you know the reason for this haste.
after: PARIS. She weeps constantly for Tybalt's death, and so I've barely talked to her about love. Venus doesn't smile in a house of mourning. Now her father thinks it's dangerous for her to give in so completely to grief. In his wisdom, he's rushing our marriage to stop the flood of her tears, hoping company will turn her thoughts from the grief she dwells on alone. Now you know the reason for this haste.

before: [Aside.]
after: [Friar Lawrence speaks the first words aside.]

before: FRIAR LAWRENCE. I wish I didn't know why it should be delayed. Look, sir, here comes the lady toward my cell.
after: FRIAR LAWRENCE. I wish I didn't know why it should be delayed. [To Paris.] Look, sir, here comes the lady toward my cell.

before: CAPULET. Send for the Count! Go tell him about this! I'll have this marriage arranged for tomorrow morning!
after: CAPULET. Send for the Count and tell him! I'll have them tie the knot tomorrow morning!

before: CAPULET. Come on, hurry, hurry! The rooster has crowed twice. The curfew bell has rung. It's three in the morning. See to the baked goods, good Angelica. Spare no expense.
after: CAPULET. Come on, hurry, hurry! The cock has crowed twice, the bell has rung, and it's three in the morning. See to the meat pies, good Angelica. Spare no expense.

before: LADY CAPULET. Yes, you were quite the night owl in your time. But I'll keep you from that kind of late-night activity now.
after: LADY CAPULET. Yes, you used to chase women at night. But I'll keep watch on that sort of hunting now.

before: [Enter Nurse.]
after: [Juliet lies on the bed. The Nurse enters.]

before: CAPULET. Ready to go, but never to return. Oh, son, the night before your wedding day, Death has taken your bride. There she lies — a flower, taken by Death. Death is my son-in-law, death is my heir. Death has married my daughter. I will die and leave him everything. Life, living — it all belongs to death now.
after: CAPULET. Ready to go, but never to return. Son, the night before your wedding, Death went to bed with your bride. There she lies, a flower that he deflowered. Death is my son-in-law, Death my heir. He has married my daughter. I'll die and leave him everything. My life, my livelihood, it all belongs to Death.

before: FIRST MUSICIAN. Well, we might as well pack up our instruments and go.
after: FIRST MUSICIAN. Well, we might as well pack up our pipes and go.

before: FIRST MUSICIAN. That it is, truly. Though the situation could be improved.
after: FIRST MUSICIAN. A sorry case indeed. Our instrument case could do with some mending too.

before: PETER. Oh, musicians, because my heart itself is playing "My Heart Is Full of Sorrow." Oh, play me some cheerful tune to comfort me.
after: PETER. Musicians, my heart is already playing 'My Heart Is Full.' Play me a jolly lament to cheer me up.

before: FIRST MUSICIAN. No cheerful tunes from us. This is no time for music.
after: FIRST MUSICIAN. No lament from us. This is no time to play.

before: FRIAR JOHN. I went to find a fellow friar to go with me. I found him here in the city, visiting the sick. But the city health officials, suspecting that we'd both been in a house infected with the plague, sealed the doors and wouldn't let us leave. So I was prevented from traveling to Mantua.
after: FRIAR JOHN. I went to find a barefoot brother of our order to go with me. He was here in town, visiting the sick. The town officials suspected we'd both been in a plague-stricken house. They sealed the doors and wouldn't let us out. That's what stopped my journey to Mantua.

before: FRIAR LAWRENCE. Now I must go to the tomb alone. Within three hours, Juliet will wake up. She'll be furious with me that Romeo hasn't heard about the plan. But I'll write to Mantua again and keep her in my cell until Romeo comes. Poor living girl, locked in a dead man's tomb!
after: FRIAR LAWRENCE. Now I must go to the tomb alone. Within three hours, Juliet will wake up. She'll be furious with me that Romeo hasn't heard about the plan. But I'll write to Mantua again and keep her in my cell until Romeo comes. Poor living corpse, locked in a dead man's tomb!

before: ROMEO. Enter, at the other end of the Churchyard, Friar Lawrence, with a lantern, crow, and spade.
after: [At the far end of the churchyard, Friar Lawrence enters with a lantern, a crowbar and a spade.]

before: [Within.] Lead, boy. Which way?]
after: FIRST WATCH. [Offstage.] Lead the way, boy. Which way?

before: FIRST WATCH. THIRD WATCH. Here's a Friar, trembling, sighing, and weeping. We took this pickaxe and this spade from him as he was coming from this side of the churchyard.
after: THIRD WATCH. Here's a Friar, trembling, sighing, and weeping. We took this pickaxe and this spade from him as he was coming from this side of the churchyard.

before: FIRST WATCH. Here is a Friar, and Romeo's slain servant, carrying tools suitable for opening the tombs of the dead.
after: FIRST WATCH. Here's a friar and the servant of the murdered Romeo. They had tools fit to break open the tombs of the dead.

before: BALTHASAR. I brought my master news of Juliet's death. He immediately rode from Mantua to this very place, to this very tomb. He gave me this letter early on and told me to deliver it to his father. Then he threatened me with death if I didn't leave and let him be.
after: BALTHASAR. I brought my master news that Juliet had died. He rode straight from Mantua to this tomb. He told me to take this letter to his father early in the morning. As he went into the tomb he threatened to kill me if I didn't leave him alone.

before: CAPULET. Oh, brother Montague, give me your hand. This is my daughter's marriage gift — I can ask for nothing more.
after: CAPULET. Brother Montague, give me your hand. That's the marriage settlement I ask for my daughter. I can ask no more.
